list.listitem: Adhere to standard recommendations regarding prenatal and perinatal screening and prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal prevention of mental retardation. A

The diagnostic yield of clinical assessment ranges from 17.2% to 34.2%. For patients without specific clinical features, clinicians should adopt a selective approach by using clinical diagnostic checklists. C
When clinical assessment fails to determine the underlying diagnosis, reassess at 3- to 6-month intervals. C
Early intervention and education programs for children with conditions that are associated with developmental delay have been shown to be beneficial. B

background.definition: Mental retardation is defined by low intellectual functioning (IQ <70) and difficulty in adaptive behavior manifesting before the patient is 18 years old. In 2013, the American Psychiatric Association (APA), which publishes the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5, APA 2013) replaced the terminology from mental retardation to intellectual disability (ID). The American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD; formerly AAMR—American Association on Mental Retardation) has also undergone an official name change.

list.listitem: A population-based study found the prevalence of ID to be 14.3 per 1000 (95% CI, 13.8-14.7) in children aged 6 years to 15 years.
In developed countries, the prevalence ranges from 5.2 to 12.2/1000, with mild and moderate ID being more common than severe ID.

Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that the prevalence of any developmental disability increased by 17.1% from 1997 to 2008 to about 1 in 6 children. The prevalence of any disability (1997-2008) was 13.87% including 7.66% who had learning disabilities and 3.65% classified as other developmental delay.

Using the most recent data from the 2009 to 2017 National Health Interview Survey of parents of children 3 to 17 years, there were significant increases in the prevalence of any developmental disability (16.2%-17.8%), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (8.5%-9.5%), autism spectrum disorder (1.1%-2.5%, P < .001), and intellectual disability (0.9%-1.2%), but a significant decrease for other causes of developmental delay (4.7% to 4.1%).

Children with ID are more likely than nonaffected children to be admitted to the hospital in the first 5 years of life (RR = 1.64; 95% CI, 1.6-1.7), on more occasions (5.3 vs. 2.2 admissions), for longer periods (29.6 vs. 8.3 days), and for a larger range of clinical diagnoses.
The average lifetime costs per person with ID have been estimated as US$1,014,000.

In a systematic review, the most common chronic health conditions in children with ID were epilepsy (22.0/100), cerebral palsy (19.8/100), anxiety disorder (17.1/100), oppositional defiant disorder (12.4/100), Down syndrome (11.0/100), and autistic disorder (10.1/100). These prevalence rates are much higher than in the general population.
Based on a systematic review of 17 studies, children with ID also display deficits in fundamental movement skills such as balance, running and throwing.
The proportion of cases of ID with a biomedical etiology varies from 16% to 75% depending on how biomedical etiology is defined.

The Finnish etiologic classification of ID/DD/GDD is based on the timing and type of injury to the CNS (). Etiologies include genetic, idiopathic, CNS malformation, external prenatal disorders, perinatal disorders, and postnatal disorders.
Down syndrome: 8% to 20% of ID, 1.1 in 1000 births.
Fragile X syndrome: 1 in 4000 male births.
Rett syndrome: 1 in 8500 female births.

Among 196 boys with dystrophinopathies (muscle weakness disorders) enrolled in a treatment trial, 28% had learning difficulties and 39% had speech delay. Neurodevelopmental problems were not associated with DMD deletion, duplication, or point mutation subtype but were associated with mutations downstream of DMD exon 45.
Maternal exposures (particularly alcohol, but also smoking) are also implicated and it has been estimated that maternal smoking on its own could account for 0.5% of ID.

Based on a meta-analysis of 13 and 10 studies, respectively, maternal diabetes during pregnancy was associated with lower pooled gross and fine motor development and a trend towards decreased language abilities in their offspring.

Perinatal exposure to endocrine disruptors (eg, phthalates, polychlorinated biphenyls [PCBs], and polycyclic aromatized hydrocarbons) is also associated with ID as well as autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, global developmental delay, and communication disorders. These compounds act by modifying actions of endogenous hormones, stimulating or inhibiting their production, changing the way they travel through the body or altering their functions.
Valproate in higher doses is associated with an increased risk of ID.
Malformations

Among studies of patients with a critical congenital heart defect without underlying genetic anomalies unergoing surgical repair, 12% of papers reported abnormal mean motor developmental scores, with the highest prevalence and severity of motor delay among children with hypoplastic left heart syndrome.

Maternal socioeconomic status (lowest 10% compared with highest 10%)

list.listitem: Routine prenatal and perinatal screening according to national guidelines for common or important causes of ID is recommended. A

Prevention should include interventions in the prenatal period (eg, Rubella immunization before pregnancy, folic acid supplementation, alcohol avoidance), perinatal period (eg, screening for infections) and postnatal period (eg, avoiding heavy metal exposure, early developmental programs). A
Developmental screening is recommended, although the optimal timing and screening method(s) is unclear. B
Prenatal screening, which may detect structural and chromosomal anomalies, includes prenatal ultrasounds and maternal serum screening for Down syndrome and other conditions.
Universal newborn screening may detect some causes of ID for which treatment is available in the form of medicines or special diets, such as hypothyroidism, phenylketonuria, and galactosemia.

Developmental screening is recommended at well-child visits (see using the history and physical below). In an RCT conducted in 4 urban pediatric practices including 2103 children, developmental screening using specific screening tools, when compared with developmental surveillance using milestones, resulted in more children being identified with delays (23.0% and 26.8% vs. 13.0%) and more children being referred to and eligible for early intervention services (7.0% and 5.3% vs. 3.0%).

In another RCT of 152 primarily Hispanic children ages 12-42 months, developmental screening conducted via telephone by a trained care coordinator vs. usual care resulted in more children being referred for developmental evaluation (32% vs. 9%, respectively) and more children receiving services (16% vs. 1%, respectively).

Prenatal prevention includes universal Rubella immunization for women before pregnancy, folic acid supplementation for women of child-bearing age, and prenatal counseling to reduce alcohol and drug abuse during pregnancy.
Perinatal prevention includes screening and treating pregnant women for infections such as syphilis.

In a systematic review of health and nutritional interventions, authors found benefit of food and micronutrient supplementation for mothers to reduce the risk of infants who are small for gestational age and iodine deficiency.
Postnatal prevention includes preventing children from heavy metal exposure (lead, mercury) and the universal iodization of salt.
Brain damage can be prevented by the provision of neonatal intensive care to very sick children, especially the extremely low birth weight babies.

A systematic review of 5 studies with 6145 fetuses found evidence to support the use of antenatal magnesium to prevent neurological abnormalities in premature infants. However, a follow-up study of 669 children of mean age 8.4 years whose mothers participated in a RCT of neuroprotection using intravenous magnesium sulfate administered during pregnancies at imminent risk of birth before 30 weeks’ gestation, did not find differences between the groups in the number of children with cerebral palsy or in the severity of cerebral palsy. There was a trend towards a lower mortality rate in the magnesium group. The initial findings at 2 years were no significant difference in outcomes of children with cerebral palsy, but a reduction in major motor dysfunction in the treated group.

Similarly, use of prophylactic early high-dose recombinant human erythropoietin in very preterm infants did not confer benefit for neurodevelopmental outcomes at 2 years in an RCT of 448 infants (365 [81%] available for follow-up).

Studies of developmental care in the NICU have not shown an impact on cognition, but have shown other benefits. Early use of continuous positive airway pressure, early surfactant administration, or higher- vs. lower-oxygen-saturation target did not influence subsequent death and neurodevelopmental impairment among randomized extremely premature infants.

Programs that emphasize early developmental interventions after hospital discharge have been shown to improve long-term cognitive outcomes in preterm infants that persist into preschool age. The effect was not sustained at school age. Motor outcomes were improved only during infancy, but long-term data are limited.

Authors of a systematic review found that motor interventions delivered to preterm infants improved motor skills, especially at 3 months, but a positive effect was seen for motor skills up to 24 months' corrected age.
Prompt treatment for meningitis during childhood can reduce the chance and extent of brain damage.
Universal newborn screening can lead to early detection and treatment of hypothyroidism, phenylketonuria, and galactosemia to prevent ID.
The diagnostic yield of clinical assessment ranges from 17.2% to 34.2%. B

For patients who do not have specific clinical features, clinicians should adopt a selective approach by using clinical diagnostic checklists that could increase the diagnostic yield of investigations. C Use of a formal developmental assessment may increase the ability to diagnose children with cognitive and communication impairments. B
When clinical assessment fails to determine the underlying diagnosis, reassess at 3- to 6-month intervals. C

ID is defined as low intellectual functioning as measured by IQ test (2 standard deviations below mean IQ; IQ <70) and difficulties in adaptive behavior that manifest before the patient is 18 years old.

The IQ of a child younger than 5 years cannot be measured by standardized intellectual tests. Instead, children younger than 5 years are evaluated according to 5 different developmental domains: (1) gross motor; (2) fine motor; (3) language or speech; (4) cognition; (5) social or personal or activities of daily living. Global developmental delay is defined as a significant delay (≥2 standard deviations) in 2 or more developmental domains.

A thorough history, physical examination, a 3-generation family pedigree, and specific behavioral assessment may help to diagnose the etiology of ID in between 17.2% and 34.2% of patients. Serial clinical photographs or videos are important complementary tools in documenting dysmorphic features, gait, seizures, movement disorders, and behavioral phenotypes.

History includes prenatal history (prenatally acquired or pregnancy-related complications), perinatal history (asphyxia, infection, prematurity), newborn screen, developmental regression, environmental risk factors (lead, mercury), and seizure.

Physical examination includes an assessment of growth parameters (body weight, body height, and head circumference); dysmorphic features; major/minor malformations; skin (cafe au lait [neurofibromatosis], ash leaf/hypopigmentation (tuberous sclerosis), hyperpigmentation (incontinentia pigmenti), port-wine stain (Sturge-Weber); neurology (hypotonia, spasticity, dystonia, ataxia, involuntary movement, weakness, cranial nerve defects, sensory defects); behavior (autistic behaviors [Rett syndrome, Fragile X syndrome, Angelman syndrome]); stereotypic behaviors (Rett syndrome); "cocktail personality" (Willliam syndrome); anxious, self-injurious, aggressive, hyperactive, and psychotic behaviors; and vision and hearing.

An abnormal infant sucking pattern in moderately and late preterm infants in one study was associated with significantly lower Mental Development and Psychomotor Development Indices on the Bayley Scales of Infant Development at 6 months corrected age (RR 3.67; 95% CI, 1.42-9.45).
The pedigree should include family history of any specific disease or chromosomal disorder, and consanguinity (risk of recessive disorder or inborn error of metabolism).
Clinical assessment may lead directly to the diagnosis in some patients who have very specific clinical features (eg, Down syndrome ).
For other patients, adopt a selective approach by using clinical diagnostic checklists that could increase the diagnostic yield of laboratory tests. See and topic on Fragile X syndrome.
Based on a cohort study, a 36-month Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ) score threshold of 270 was optimal for identifying children with an IQ <85 at 5 to 6 years.

Authors of a systematic review of 36 studies of administration of the ASQ to children 12 to 60 months of age followed by conduct of a formal behavioral assessment within 2 months of questionnaire administration found a moderate accuracy for the ASQ in identifying children with developmental, motor, cognitive, and language delays (area under the curve [AUC] 0.75 for 1 SD below the age-specific mean and 0.87 for 2 SD below the age-specific mean). If a child passes all domains, there is a moderate probability the child does not have a severe delay.

For children with an established diagnosis of delay in a specific area or general areas of development, a rough estimate of the overall developmental quotient ([developmental age/chronological age] × 100) and developmental quotient in each of the 5 domains should be made during each clinical evaluation (see ).

In a study of 190 children in England born at <30 weeks gestation who were attending routine clinical follow-up at post-term ages 20-28 months, following a set of key questions designed to be used without formal training or developmental testing was successful in identification of a child’s status as no impairment or no severe impairment (specificities 83.9%-100.0% and 96.6%-100.0%, respectively). Identification of cognitive and communication impairments, however, was poor compared to assessment using the Bayley Scales of Infant Development.

For patients where comprehensive clinical assessment fails to provide the underlying diagnosis there are three possible options: (1) await clinical evolution, and proceed to some selected investigations and reassess at 3-month to 6-month intervals; (2) consult experts, such as pediatricians, clinical geneticists, dysmorphologists, or child neurologists; and (3) use library/computer/web-based search for possible syndromal diagnosis.
The prevalence of causes of ID/DD in the patient's population is very important in interpreting the diagnostic evaluation.

Routine cytogenetic testing is recommended for children with unexplained ID/DD (diagnostic yield 3.7%-9.5%), but is more likely to be diagnostic with two or more dysmorphic features (20%). Subtelomeric testing may be considered in children with unexplained moderate/severe ID/DD (4.4%-6.6%), but is more likely to be diagnostic when used selectively (see ). Fragile X testing may be considered in boys with unexplained ID/DD (2%-2.6%; 3.9% in males), but is more likely to be diagnostic when used selectively (7.6%).

In an update of the Treatable ID app, investigators identified 116 treatable inherited metabolic disorders (139 genes) presenting with global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Most disorders were treated with nutritional, pharmacological and vitamin and trace element supplementation.
Testing using chromosomal microarray (CMA) and fragile X testing is recommended by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (2010).

In a Chinese study of 410 samples submitted for CMA and karyotyping, 61 (14.9%) had chromosomal abnormalities identified using CMA and 47 (11.5%) had chromosomal abnormalities identified using karyotyping. Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed that the AUC for CMA on the diagnosis of chromosomal abnormalities was 0.93 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and for karyotyping was 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.93); the combination of CMA and karyotyping could improve diagnosis.

Given recent advances in genetic testing, authors of a multidisciplinary group using a meta-analysis of 30 papers reached consensus that exome sequencing was superior to CMA in diagnostic yield for neurodevelopmental disorders (overall yield 35% vs. 15% to 20%, respectively). In this study, medical management changed in 30% of those with a diagnosis by ES. The exome, which makes up about 1.5% of the entire human genome, are the protein-coding regions of genes.

Metabolic disease is less common. Therefore, after initial clinical assessment, a staged approach with a screening panel followed by definitive metabolic tests should be adopted to increase the likelihood of detection. The latter are often costly and may involve invasive procedures like biopsies.
Neuroimaging is of limited use as the initial work-up of unselected patients with ID/DD.

Vision assessment tools including Lea Grating Acuity Test, Lea fixation stick, Lea puzzle and Lea playing cards can be used for children from birth to 2.5 years. Other tests for older children are outlined in the reference provided

Early intervention and education programs for children with conditions associated with developmental delay have proven beneficial. B
Treat any underlying conditions (eg, hypothyroidism or inborn errors of metabolism).

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is more common among persons with ID. Authors of a systematic review found a single small study of amphetamine for patients with Fragile X (no benefit seen), and 11 studies of risperidone but none of sufficient quality to assess.

Antipsychotic use in individuals with intellectual and/or developmental disability causes greater weight gain compared with placebo (mean difference 1.10 kg; 95% CI, 0.79-1.40; I2 = 54%; OR 3.94; 95% CI, 2.15-7.23).

In a Russian RCT of 87 children aged 6-12 months with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and psychomotor developmental delay, use of hopantenic acid syrup twice daily for 2 months resulted in a significant decrease in developmental delay in the intervention group vs. usual care (63.6% vs. 36.4%) without significant adverse effects. The drug, also known as N-pantoyl-GABA, is a central nervous system depressant. There is a case report of an episode of acute encephalopathy in a child with Rett syndrome given hopantenic acid.
For adolescents with ID, menstrual intervention or suppression may be warranted. The American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists have prepared a bulletin to provide guidance to clinicians.
Acupuncture and other alternative therapies have been tried with no evidence to support efficacy.

In one RCT with 146 children, melatonin was useful for improving sleep latency but did not appear to result in an important increase in sleep (22.4 minutes [95% CI, 0.5-44.3 minutes]) or in child behavior or family functioning.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 studies of overweight or obese children with intellectual disabilities using primarily physical activity interventions found no benefit on weight but significant effects on 6-minute walk distance (51.86 m; 95% CI, 16.49-87.22).

In an RCT of 30 children with intellectual disabilities and developmental coordination disorder, 8-weeks of combined physio-hemsball training improved postural control and dynamic and postural balance compared to a control group.
One small RCT of a 20-week occupational therapy program of 15-minute sessions for children with ID demonstrated benefit on fine motor skills and parental satisfaction with performance.
Massage therapy, twice weekly for 12 weeks, resulted in improved motor scores and sensory sensitivity behavior in the 18 1- to 3-year-old children randomized to treatment vs. controls.

Early intervention programs are usually composed of different types of services targeted for disabled children to enhance their developmental competence. Although interpretation of available efficacy studies is limited by their methodologies, there is growing consensus based on best available evidence that early intervention is beneficial.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 25 studies with 3615 children born before 37-weeks gestation also found that early intervention had a small, positive influence on cognitive and motor outcomes during infancy, with cognitive benefits persisting into preschool age based on a few studies.

As reported in a meta-analysis evaluating early intervention implemented in newborn to 3-year-old disabled children, programs that served a heterogeneous group of children, provided a structured curriculum, and targeted their efforts on parents and children together appeared to be the most effective.

Authors of a systematic review of 48 articles identified 24 primary-care interventions categorized as general developmental support, general behavioral development, or topic-specific interventions (eg, colic, reading-focused). These included individual or group sessions to review videotaped vignettes, direct videotaping and review, newsletters, and meeting with a developmental specialist). Many studies reported positive effects on child development and parenting behaviors. Details of specific intervention outcomes are summarized in the paper.
Authors of a systematic review of 15 papers found insufficient evidence that video games improved motor outcomes in children with developmental coordination disorder.
Evidence for parent training support is limited but promising.

In one RCT of parent-implemented early language intervention for 2-year-old late talkers, there was higher growth in expressive vocabulary in children in the intervention group at age 3 years, but no differences between intervention and control groups at age 4 years. Expressive syntax remained below that of their peers in both groups, and 29% of the children had expressive language scores below the mean range.

Authors of a systematic review of 18 studies found support for use of heritage languages in addition to the majority language for improving outcomes for bilingual individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders.

In an RCT of 110 adolescents with intellectual and developmental disabilities (aged ∼16 years, 53% female, BMI 33) those randomized to the enhanced stop light diet compared to a conventional meal plan experienced significantly greater weight loss (-5.0 ± 5.9 kg vs. -1.8 ± 4.0 kg). The stop light diet used a stop light guide, enhanced with portion-controlled meals. Weight loss did not differ by delivery strategy which was either face-to-face or offered by remote delivery.

With respect to oral health for children with intellectual disability, fluoride interventions may provide long-term reductions in caries and chlorhexidine may provide short-term and long-term reductions in plaque and gingivitis, based on low-certainty evidence.

Gene therapy was used in six children ages 4-19 years with aromatic l-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) deficiency which causes a decrease in catecholamines and serotonin levels in the brain leads to developmental delay and movement disorders. At two years, there was marked improvement in motor function.
Preclinical gene therapy studies continue.

For consecutive children born before 27 weeks gestation in Sweden who received perinatal care vs. control group born at term, of the 69% who survived to 2.5 years, 73% had mild (31%) or no (42%) disability and 11% had severe disability measured at a mean of 30.5 months. Neurodevelopmental outcomes improved over time.

In a more recent Swedish study of over 1.5 million births (1973-1997), 149,065 children (5.8%) were born preterm with an overall survival to at least 18 years of 94.2%; most (54.6% vs. 63% for term infants) had no major comorbidities as defined by the Adolescent and Young Adult Health Outcomes and Patient Experience survey and 73.1% (vs. 81.8% for term infants) had no major comorbidities as defined by the Charlson Comorbidity Index.

In an Australian study of children born prior to 28 weeks gestation, survival was similar (63.4%) but most children had some neurobehavioral impairment at age 8 years (71% vs. 42% among control children), and one-half of subjects had multiple impairments.

In a longitudinal study of 376 early preterm, 688 born moderately-late preterm, and 403 full term-born children, developmental problems, assessed using the ASQ total score, were identified in 13%, 7.9% and 4.1%, respectively at age 4 years. One year later, similar rates were demonstrated for moderately-late preterm and full term-born children (7.3% and 4.8%, respectively), but significantly higher rates of developmental problems were seen among early preterm children (16.2%).

In a study of 29 very preterm-born individuals (<32 weeks' gestation) and 25 term-born controls followed longitudinally at 7-12 years of age and again at 13-16 years of age, children born prematurely showed significantly stronger improvement of inhibition and cognitive flexibility between childhood and adolescence than term-born children who worsened more often (36%) in the domain of inhibition than the preterm group (14%).

Among newborns with severe hyperbilirubinemia (TSB ranging 33.5-38 mg/dL; 573-650 µmol/L), the BIND score (assessing mental status, muscle tone, and cry patterns) was predictive of neurologic and auditory impairment at at 3 to 5 months of age. All infants with severe encephalopathy (BIND scores 7-9) either died or suffered residual neurologic and auditory impairment compared to 62.5% of infants with a BIND score of 4 to 6 and 1% of infants with lower BIND scores.

Cranial ultrasound was useful for predicting adverse developmental outcomes in one follow-up study of 129 very preterm infants. Grades 2 or 3 at first ultrasound were associated with adverse mental (OR 3.2 and OR 3.78) and motor (OR 2.25 and OR 2.59) development.
Frontal lobe lesions identified on magnetic resonance imaging predicted adverse 18-month cognitive and language development.

MRI injury scores were also associated with neurodevelopmental outcome at 18-22 months among 128 infants ≥36 weeks of gestation with moderate-severe neonatal encephalopathy. The adjusted odds of death or severe disability increased 3.7-fold (95% CI, 1.8-7.9) for each increment of injury score and the AUC for severe MRI patterns to predict death or severe disability was 0.77. Agreement between reviewers of the MRI, however, was only moderate (weighted kappa 0.56) and positive and negative predictive values were 36% and 100%, respectively.

In addition, authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies found that diffuse excessive high signal intensity on term equivalent-age MRI was not predictive of future development of cognitive disabilities (summary AUC 0.54; 95% CI, 0.50-0.58).
Amplitude-integrated EEG showing any background abnormality within the first 7 days of life was a predictor of abnormal neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Provide information about natural history, including likely health-related problems, behavioral phenotype, and life expectancy.
Provide information about family support associations.
Provide information about the condition that is important for service providers.
Provide genetic counseling, including preconception counseling.

feature.caption: Etiological Classification of Developmental and Intellectual Delay Based on Timing and Mechanism of CNS Injury.
feature.feature_body:
Genetic
Chromosomal anomalies (numerical anomalies): trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), XO (Turner syndrome) Chromosomal anomalies (structural anomalies): chromosomal translocation, deletion, ring chromosome, or inversion Subchromosomal (subtelomeric): 4p-/Wolf-Hirschlorn syndrome,* 5p-/Cri-du-chat syndrome* Subchormosomal (contiguous gene syndrome/ microdeletion): Prader-Willi syndrome, Angelman syndrome, William syndrome Monogenic disorders (autosomal dominant): Tuberous sclerosis, Noonan syndrome Monogenic disorders (autosomal recessive): Inborn errors of metabolism Monogenic disorders (x-linked): Fragile X, Rett syndrome Monogenic disorders (mitochondrial): MELAS, Leigh's disease Polygenic predisposition/syndrome presumed to be genetic: Kabuki syndrome, hypomelanosis of Ito, Goldenhar syndrome, VACTERL syndrome
CNS malformation
Holoprosencephaly Lissencephaly
External prenatal disorders
Congenital infection: rubella, CMV, and HIV Medications/toxin: alcohol, smoking, and valproate Nutrition/IUGR/prematurity Diabetes Radiation Others
Perinatal disorders
Infection: meningitis, herpes Delivery: asphyxia, trauma Others: hypoglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia
Postnatal disorders
Infection: meningitis, encephalitis Other CNS damage: tumor, hypoxia, and toxins Psychosocial problems: deprivation
Unknown/idiopathic Can be associated with other conditions (eg, cerebral palsy, epilepsy, or autism) *These examples can be classified under chromosomal or subtelomeric, depending on the size of deletion and whether these can be picked up microscopically by conventional karyotype or submicroscopically by subtelomeric FISH technique. From Wilska ML, Kaski MK. Why and how to assess the aetiological diagnosis of children with intellectual disability/mental retardation and other neurodevelopmental disorders: description of the Finnish approach. Eur J Paediatr Neurol 2001;5:7-13.

feature.caption: Subtelomeric Deletion Syndrome. Selective Approach Using a 5-Item Checklist. (This scoring system has been based on 22 cases of diagnosed subtelomeric deletion syndrome in 2002; the score has not been validated.)
feature.feature_body:
Items Points
1. Family history of ID
- Compatible with Mendelian inheritance 1
- Incompatible with Mendelian inheritance(including discordant phenotypes) 2
2. Prenatal onset growth retardation 2
3. Postnatal growth abnormalities (1 point for each of the following, up to 2 points) Microcephaly (1) Short stature (1) Macrocephaly (1) Tall stature (1)
0 to 2
4. Two or more facial dysmorphic features (hypertelorism, nasal anomalies, and/or ear anomalies) 2
5. Nonfacial dysmorphism and congenital abnormalities (1 point for each anomaly, up to 2 points) Hand anomaly (1) Heart anomaly (1) Hypospadias ± undescended testis (1)
0 to 2
